rationale: A wins because it has the same real core stories as B, but better risk control: “This is not an angle to pitch proactively... it is the question REI must be ready to answer” is the line that keeps a founder from wandering into a labor story smiling. B is competent, but “competitors get benchmarked against” and “The prevailing belief this cuts against” add thesis before the proof is in. That is the small but expensive difference between strategic angles and tidy pitch bait.
gaps_in_A: “Your old tent now has a trade-in price at the local REI” invents a gear category; the update never says tents are accepted or how credit is priced.
“every store has to staff and stock” overstates the facts; the update says trade-ins and repairs are available at every store, not that each store has onsite repair labor or used-gear inventory.
“had its best year for members” gets ahead of the record-dividend fact; a largest-ever dividend may reflect membership growth, dividend formula, or dollars, not necessarily the best member year.
gaps_in_B: “competitors get benchmarked against” imports a competitive-frame claim the update does not supply.

“The prevailing belief this cuts against: a member-owned co-op is assumed to be the worker- and community-friendly alternative to corporate retail” needs outside proof; otherwise it is a contrarian angle built on a straw assumption.
“resale is real infrastructure” is too strong while the used-gear sales share is explicitly undisclosed; keep it to operational rollout unless REI gives adoption data.

Refusing “REI customer saves money buying used gear — a shopper's story” as pure hallucination throws away a workable local feature shape; the savings claim is unsupported, but a conditional member/repair walk-through angle is valid.
